$comment:
Ed25519 verification vectors, v0.

WHY A CORPUS FOR A PRIMITIVE.
The two SDKs verify Ed25519 by different routes, and they have to. The Node SDK
hands the work to OpenSSL through node:crypto. The Python SDK cannot: `pip
install aegis-trust` is dependency-free by contract
(python/tests/test_lite_zero_dep.py pins it), Python has no Ed25519 in its
standard library, and adding a crypto dependency to the LITE path so that a
small number of users can verify an attestation would break the invariant for
everyone else. So python/src/aegis_trust/_ed25519.py implements RFC 8032
verification in `int` arithmetic.

Two implementations of one primitive is exactly the condition in which they
quietly stop agreeing. This file is where the agreement is written down, and
both read it:

  python/tests/test_ed25519_corpus.py
  node/tests/ed25519Corpus.test.ts

WHAT IS IN HERE.
  - The four RFC 8032 section 7.1 known-answer vectors. These are the only
    inputs in this repo whose correct answer was decided by someone other than
    us.
  - A real ed25519-dalek signature over a real Core attestation's canonical
    message, straight out of the shipped aegis-gateway binary. An
    implementation that passed the RFC vectors and still disagreed with dalek
    in practice would fail here.
  - Rejection vectors for each failure class that matters: a flipped message
    bit, a flipped bit in each half of the signature (R and S take different
    code paths), a substituted key, a signature from a different key, an
    all-zero signature, wrong lengths in both directions, a non-canonical
    public-key encoding (y = p + 1), and the unreduced scalar S + L.

THE ONE WORTH READING TWICE.
`unreduced-scalar-s-plus-l` satisfies the verification equation. A verifier
that omits the S < L check of RFC 8032 section 5.1.7 accepts it, and then a
single message has two valid signatures by the same key — which breaks anything
that treats a signature as an identifier. Both implementations reject it:
OpenSSL enforces the canonical scalar, and the Python code checks explicitly.
That was measured, not assumed, before this vector was added.

SIGNING IS NOT HERE, AND MUST NOT BE.
There is no signing code in either SDK. Verification touches only public values,
so the Python implementation's lack of constant-time behaviour costs nothing; a
signing counterpart would handle a secret scalar in Python `int` arithmetic and
leak it through timing. The asymmetry is the reason the verification half is
safe to hand-implement and the signing half never would be.

WHAT THIS CORPUS DOES NOT SETTLE.
Small-order public keys are accepted by both implementations, because OpenSSL
accepts them and a divergence about what "valid" means would be worse than the
property is worth here. Nothing depends on it: the attestation verifier pins the
expected public key by value, so a small-order key could only be reached by an
operator pinning one.

vectors.doc: RFC 8032 section 7.1 known-answer vector. Must verify.
RFC 8032 section 7.1 known-answer vector. Must verify.
RFC 8032 section 7.1 known-answer vector. Must verify.
RFC 8032 section 7.1 known-answer vector. Must verify.
RFC vector 2 with one bit flipped in the message. Must NOT verify.
One bit flipped in the R half of the signature. The R and S halves take different code paths (point decompression vs scalar reduction), so both are exercised.
One bit flipped in the S half of the signature. Must NOT verify.
One bit flipped in the public key — the attacker-substitutes-a-key shape at the primitive level.
RFC vector 3's signature offered against RFC vector 2's key.
64 zero bytes. R decodes to the identity and S is zero — the degenerate input a verifier that only length-checked would accept.

The malleability window RFC 8032 section 5.1.7 closes: S replaced by S+L, which satisfies the verification equation but is not a canonical scalar. A verifier without the S < L check accepts it, and then one message has two valid signatures. Both SDKs must reject it — OpenSSL does, and the Python implementation checks explicitly.
A public key whose y coordinate is p+1 — outside the field, so the encoding is not canonical. Rejected rather than silently reduced.
65 bytes — a trailing byte a length-tolerant verifier would ignore.

A real ed25519-dalek signature over a real Core attestation's canonical message, produced by the shipped aegis-gateway binary. A primitive that passed the RFC vectors but disagreed with dalek in practice would still fail here.
The same real signature against a canonical message with a single byte changed — the whole point of signing the message rather than trusting the JSON.
